question: A medical student receives three doses of hepatitis B vaccine. Post-vaccination serology shows: anti-HBs 85 mIU/mL, HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative. What is the correct interpretation?

answers.text: Successful vaccination with protective immunity — anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL without anti-HBc confirms vaccine-induced immunity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Vaccination generates ONLY anti-HBs (from recombinant HBsAg). Absence of anti-HBc confirms no natural infection occurred (anti-HBc requires exposure to core antigen, absent in the vaccine). Anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL is the defined protective threshold.

answers.text: Acute hepatitis B in the window period

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Window period is defined by anti-HBc IgM as the sole detectable marker (HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet appeared). This student has anti-HBs present and no anti-HBc — completely inconsistent with window period.

answers.text: Chronic hepatitis B carrier state with low-level replication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A chronic carrier must be HBsAg positive. This student is HBsAg negative with protective anti-HBs — the exact opposite serological pattern.

answers.text: Natural infection followed by recovery and immunity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Natural infection produces BOTH anti-HBs AND anti-HBc (because the immune system encounters surface and core antigens during infection). The absence of anti-HBc here confirms vaccine-induced immunity without prior natural exposure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key distinction: vaccine → anti-HBs only (no core antigen in vaccine); natural infection → anti-HBs + anti-HBc (both antigens encountered). Anti-HBc is the differentiator.
Vaccine-induced immunity: anti-HBs positive (≥10 mIU/mL), all other markers negative. Natural immunity: anti-HBs AND anti-HBc both positive.
